entries.title: US arrests right-wing provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos
entries.summary: Yiannopoulos, a right-wing commentator, was an early supporter of President Trump and his immigration crackdown, but they have since fallen out. DHS said he was an "illegal alien" who overstayed his visit in the US.
entries.content:
August 28, 2026

Yiannopoulos, a right-wing commentator, was an early supporter of President Trump and his immigration crackdown, but they have since fallen out. DHS said he was an "illegal alien" who overstayed his visit in the US.

US authorities have detained right-wing commentator Milo Yiannopoulos and plan to deport him, the Department of Homeland Security said on Friday.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents arrested the British provocateur at New Orleans International Airport on Thursday for overstaying in the US, the department said, describing him as an "illegal alien from the United Kingdom."

Once a Donald Trump supporter and advocate of the president's immigration crackdown, Yiannopoulos has since fallen out with the Trump movement.

More to come...

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Spain asks EU's Frontex for help in processing Ceuta migrants
entries.summary: Of the over 70,000 migrants who illegally crossed into Ceuta from Morocco in late July, some 5,000 still remain in the Spanish exclave. Ceuta residents have been angrily protesting their continued presence.
entries.content:
August 28, 2026

Of the over 70,000 migrants who illegally crossed into Ceuta from Morocco in late July, some 5,000 still remain in the Spanish exclave. Ceuta residents have been angrily protesting their continued presence.

Spain has asked for help from the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) in processing migrants who crossed into Ceuta last month and still remain in the North African Spanish territory.

Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska sent a request to Beate Gminder, the European Commission's director general for migration and home affairs, to help with screening migrants in Ceuta.

Madrid has also requested 10 more Frontex officers to help with the screening.

Frontex is the European Union agency responsible for managing the bloc's external borders and fighting cross-border crime.

Why is Spain asking for help with the Ceuta migrants?

Over 70,000 migrants crossed from Morocco to Ceuta illegally in late July. The incident triggered a massive EU migration emergency and brought Spain's leftist government much criticism.

Though the majority of people were quickly sent back to Morocco, at least 5,000 migrants still remain in the Spanish territory of roughly 80,000 residents.

Madrid cannot deport the remaining migrants quickly as a collective return without individual assessment is prohibited under international law and Spanish court rulings.

Rising anger against migrants in Ceuta

Ceuta's residents loudly reject the migrants' continued presence and have made their voice heard via protests which have sometimes turned violent.

Spain has ruled out moving the migrants into the mainland as that would invite further criticism from the opposition as well as some EU members.

Migrants have set up camp on Trampolin Beach, where some tents have been attacked and set on fire amid the residents' rising anger.

On Thursday, protests turned violent with 12 migrants arrested after stoning an army vehicle, injuring one soldier and other migrants. Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that 11 migrants were expelled from the territory, citing sources from the city's main court.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Austria museum heist: Thieves snatch diamond necklace
entries.summary: The stolen necklace, studded with 673 precious stones, belonged to Egypt's Queen Nazli. It was being displayed as part of the museum's exhibition for designs by France's Van Cleef and Arpels.
entries.content:
August 28, 2026

The stolen necklace, studded with 673 precious stones, belonged to Egypt's Queen Nazli. It was being displayed as part of the museum's exhibition for designs by France's Van Cleef and Arpels.

Two men walked into Vienna's Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) as visitors only to storm out with a priceless 200-carat platinum and diamond necklace worth several million dollars, police said on Friday.

The broad-daylight heist on Thursday, the latest in a series of high-profile thefts to have hit European museums in the past year, triggered a search that grew beyond Austria's borders. 

What do we know about the heist?

The two robbers bought tickets to enter the museum.

But once inside, they made their way to the temporary exhibition for French designers Van Cleef and Arpels and "smashed a glass display case" with a hammer before "fleeing with the jewelry in an unknown direction," according to a police statement.

Police added that they did not wear masks and could be clearly seen on surveillance cameras.

A police spokeswoman told the German DPA news agency that one of the robbers was carrying what is believed to be a real firearm.

She said visitors and security staff were in the room when the display case was smashed, adding that it was understandable that the security staff did not stand in the way of the armed perpetrator.

The MAK museum confirmed the theft but did not comment further. On its website, the museum continues to promote its exhibition, which is due to run until September 27.

What do we know about the stolen necklace?

The stolen necklace belonged to Egypt's now-deposed Queen Nazli and was designed for her in 1939 for her daughter's marriage to the future Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, whose family has also since been removed from power.

It is made of platinum and 673 precious stones said to weigh over 200 carats.

Van Cleef and Arpels describes the necklace on its website as a "triumph of white jewelry."

The case is only the latest in a string of heists to have hit European museums in recent month.

The most high profile was last October's Louvre museum break-in in Paris, which saw thieves snatching in jewellery worth $102 million (roughly €88 million) in under eight minutes. Museum thefts have also been reported in Italy and Spain.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Germany news: Baltic summit plans hybrid-threat task force
entries.summary: Ministers from countries bordering the Baltic Sea have agreed on a rapid response force to counter hybrid threats. Meanwhile, the far-right AfD has failed to topple a state premier. DW has more updates from Germany.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Baltic summit plans hybrid-threat task force

Published August 28, 2026last updated August 28, 2026

Ministers from countries bordering the Baltic Sea have agreed on a rapid response force to counter hybrid threats. Meanwhile, the far-right AfD has failed to topple a state premier. DW has more updates from Germany.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

This blog is now closed. Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Friday, August 28, 2026:

  • Baltic interior ministers meeting in Germany have agreed on a task force to deal with hybrid threats
  • The AfD in Thuringia has failed to win a no-confidence vote in the state premier
  • Germany's Green Party has warned gas storage levels are far too low
  • Germany has seen its earliest-ever grape harvest after an exceptionally hot summer
  • Germany's president has paid tribute to Norway's late King Harald

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Dobrindt: Security task force and enhanced drone defense agreed at Baltic summit

Dobrindt: Security task force and enhanced drone defense agreed at Baltic summit

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt says that Baltic and European leaders at a special hybrid security meeting agreed to plans to set up a new security task force and to enhance collective drone defense capabilities. 

The assembled politicians discussed "urgent security policy questions for a shared future in the Baltic Sea region," Dobrindt said amid the meeting at the Mürwik naval training center in Flensburg on Germany's northeast coast

"Foreign powers are trying to attack our security with hybrid measures, to destabilize our democracies, to weaken our economy," he said. "Drone attacks, cyber attacks, spying, disinformation, arson attacks on critical infrastructure, covert operations and the use of 'disposable agents' are all rapidly increasing in number."

Dobrindt warned that the recent past had shown a pronounced increase in the "quality and intensity" of such attacks and surmised that "we must prepare ourselves for the hybrid threat situation continuing to intensify."

He said the shared goal was to bolster defense against such hybrid threats.

"We want to investigate, deter and defend altogether more quickly," Dobrindt said, saying they wanted to work together to transform the Balitc from a "collective risk area" into a "collective defensive area."

The assembled politicians from Germany, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Sweden, Norway and Ireland — the current holder of the rotating EU presidency — had a working lunch at the Mürwik base amid the talks.

They were also taken out on the Baltic Sea in a German Federal Police motorboat.

Skip next section Germany will stick to 'Lake Ontario' despite Trump's 'Lake America' renaming

Germany will stick to 'Lake Ontario' despite Trump's 'Lake America' renaming

Germany intends to continue referring to the body of water between the US and Canada as Lake Ontario, despite US President Donald Trump's decision to rename it as "Lake America" amid his growing rift with Canada.

"This is an American decision to refer to this lake by a different name. For the time being, it has no further implications for other countries," said a spokesman for the German Foreign Ministry on Friday. "As far as we are concerned, it remains Lake Ontario, which is the customary name."

The spokesman went on to argue that "in the US, football is called 'soccer,' but that doesn't mean it's called 'soccer' in other countries as well."

When asked whether the decision could culminate in fresh Trump resentment toward Berlin, the spokesman said that naming of waterways "should not be a reason to harbour political resentment toward anyone."

Earlier this year, Trump and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz engaged in a public rift after the German leader said the US was being "humiliated" at the negotiating table with Iran amid the war. Trump then announced a reduction in the number of US troops in Germany.

Skip next section In pictures — Gamescom 2026 in Cologne heads into weekend

In pictures — Gamescom 2026 in Cologne heads into weekend

Skip next section Berlin mayor: Hackers trying to blackmail city hall after data breach

Berlin mayor: Hackers trying to blackmail city hall after data breach

Berlin's Mayor Kai Wegner says the city-state's government is being blackmailed by hackers who breached several sectors of its administration earlier in this month.

"Berlin has become a victim of a serious crime," Wegner said, albeit adding that the state "will not allow itself to be blackmailed."

German news magazine Spiegel reports that the hackers are demanding 30 bitcoin or just over €2 million (roughly $2.3 million).

As a result of the cyber attack, departments like city planning, construction, housing, mobility, transportation and environment and climate protection were all isolated from the state government network for around a week, starting on August 14.

Among other things, it meant that it was not possible to apply for or pay out housing benefits for several days.

At first, officials said they did not believe sensitive data had been captured. Then on Wednesday of this week, the state government said it was possible that personalized or non-public information might be affected.

According to Spiegel, a ransomware group known as Rhysida is claiming responsibility in a post on the dark web, saying it had secured some 6 terabytes of data and putting a countdown to the time of its publication alongside a demand for 30 bitcoin.

Rhysida gained notoriety in 2023 when it hacked the online information systems of the British Library and published leaked material when it was not paid the bitcoin ransom it demanded.

Skip next section Finance Minister Klingbeil calls on Trump to end 'irresponsible' Iran war

Finance Minister Klingbeil calls on Trump to end 'irresponsible' Iran war

German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil is the guest on this Friday's "Interview der Woche" political podcast by public broadcaster ARD.

Much of the interview revolves around domestic policies directly in Klingbeil's ministerial wheelhouse, like the sugar tax, planned income tax reforms, and Germany's difficult economic situation more generally. 

But when the discussion turned to fuel prices in Germany, which are nearing their all-time highs from much earlier in the year once again, the Social Democrat (SPD) leader Klingbeil wasted no time in pointing to the external factors in play.

"First of all you have to say that this is the fault of Donald Trump, who started this irresponsible war in Iran," Klingbeil said. "These are the effects, which people are now feeling at the fuel pumps. Therefore the most important thing — and I will be in the US next week for the G20 finance ministers' summit — and the most important message to the US is: Bring this war to an end. That's the first point." 

Klingbeil said that the second issue should be to address oil companies "profiteering" as a result of the unrest in Iran and the Gulf, arguing that consumer prices were not a fair reflection of the oil prices or economic fundamentals.

He said he wanted the question of windfall taxes on oil companies to once again be discussed at an EU level. 

"The oil companies are making gains on the back of this geopolitical situation," Klingbeil said. "They are filling their pockets and that needs to be stopped, which is why I'm lobbying for the windfall tax and am saying that the proceeds that are raised should be redirected to consumers — which could be achieved by reducing fuel prices."

For a two-month period, Germany dipped its taxes on gasoline and diesel to try to relieve the pressure on prices at the pumps. But this measure expired without renewal in July and prices have since returned close to their highest-ever levels, from earlier in the year. Other smaller factors like the low water levels on the River Rhine impacting freight transport have also played a more minor role in driving up prices in some parts of the country. 

Skip next section Man gets life in jail for US tourist's rape, murder

Man gets life in jail for US tourist's rape, murder

A German court on Friday sentenced an 81-year-old man to life in prison for the rape and murder of a US tourist over 30 years ago.

Amy Lopez was 24 when she was raped and killed by the convicted man in 1994.

Hans S., whose last name is not given as per Germany's privacy laws, was only arrested earlier this year, when police were finally able to identify him using new DNA technology.

Read more on the 81-year-old's trial and how police managed to arrest him over three decades after the crime here.

Skip next section Football: Leverkusen, Hoffenheim, Freiburg learn European opponents

Football: Leverkusen, Hoffenheim, Freiburg learn European opponents

German Bundesliga sides Bayer Leverkusen, TSG Hoffenheim and SC Freiburg have found out their opponents in European competition for this season.

In the Europa League, Europe's second-tier international club competition, Leverkusen and Hoffenheim will both face French giants Olympique Lyon, Turkish side Besiktas and OFI from the Greek island of Crete.

The final of this year's Europa League will take place in Frankfurt — extra motivation for the German clubs to reach a final on home soil.

In the third-tier Conference League, SC Freiburg will also face Greek and Turkish opposition in the form of Panathinaikos and Trabzonspor respectively. The latter made headlines this summer when they signed Egyptian star Mohamed Salah.

Last season, Freiburg reached the final of the Europa League in Istanbul, where they lost to Aston Villa. Coincidentally, this season's Conference League final will also be in Istanbul, in the same stadium, so Freiburg will be aiming for redemption.

Skip next section Thuringia: Far-right AfD fails in no-confidence vote against state premier

Thuringia: Far-right AfD fails in no-confidence vote against state premier

The leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the eastern German state of Thuringia, Björn Höcke, failed on Friday in an attempt to topple State Premier Mario Voigt of the center-right Christian Democrats (CDU) with a vote of no-confidence.

Standing himself for the position of state premier, Höcke received only 33 votes in the 88-seat state parliament, while 49 lawmakers voted against him. There were three abstentions.

It was the second time this year that Höcke, who a German court ruled in 2019 may legally be described as a "fascist," has attempted to unseat Voigt in the Thuringian state parliament, or Landtag.

Like on the first occasion, Höcke once again argued that Voigt's recently revoked doctorate renders him unsuitable to head up the state government. Voigt had an appeal rejected by the University of Chemnitz last month, prompting Höcke's latest no-confidence vote.

"You are a plagiarist," he told Voigt, and described his coalition with the center-left  Social Democrats (SPD) and the left-wing populist BSW as a "plunder gang."

Voigt, on the other hand, said the vote in his favor was a strong show of support and told Höcke: "I won't allow you to drag me down."

The vote in Thuringia came a week ahead of key local elections in the neighboring state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD have a significant lead in the polls and could potentially form a majority far-right government.

Skip next section Star sprinter Owen Ansah to challenge NADA doping ban in court

Star sprinter Owen Ansah to challenge NADA doping ban in court

European 200 meter champion Owen Ansah plans to challenge the German Anti-Doping Agency (NADA) proposal to suspend him for failing to provide a sample on demand.

Ansah faced a 20-day deadline to accept a doping ban of four years, with a possibility of it being shortened to three, or to seek a court hearing at Germany's sports arbitration court.

NADA announced Ansah's decision on Friday as the deadline expired but said it could provide no further information on the trial or its timeline. 

The case is unusual as Ansah is not accused of failing a doping test. He's accused of refusing to provide a sample, which is treated as a direct indication of guilt.

But Ansah has previously argued that the tester came to his hotel room out of the agreed timeframe, when he was running late for a plane, and so he refused to comply. He also argues that him providing a clean sample the next day to the World Anti-Doping Agency in a separate test rendered the issue moot.

Most recently his lawyer said the sprinter would be making no further comments on the issue amid the likelihood of an appeal.

Ansah has continued to compete this summer amid the dispute, winning gold in the 200 meters at the European Championships and bronze in the 100 meters, as well as 100 and 200 meter gold in the German championships. Accepting the ban would disqualify him from these competitions retroactively.

The German with Ghanaian heritage is 25, so a lengthy suspension could effectively mean the end of his career — making it prohibitively difficult for him to maintain his performance level, and with his physical peak potentially passing amid the ban.

Skip next section German nationals missing after Nepal-China flash floods

German nationals missing after Nepal-China flash floods

A low double-digit number of German nationals are still missing after devastating flash floods along the Nepal-China border, Germany's Foreign Office said on Friday.

A German family of four has meanwhile been rescued from the disaster zone in Nepal and flown by helicopter with other survivors to an army camp in Battar Bazar, according to the German Press Agency (dpa).

German embassies in Kathmandu and Beijing are working with the families of those missing and local authorities to establish their whereabouts.

"The full extent of these flash floods is still very difficult to assess," a Foreign Office spokesperson said in Berlin, adding that the situation in the affected region remained "very, very unclear."

Nepal's tourism authorities had earlier reported eight German nationals missing. Four were part of a group of foreign pilgrims returning from a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar in Tibet when contact with them was lost.

The death toll from Wednesday's flash floods has risen to at least 543.

Skip next section Germany risks missing 2026 climate target

Germany risks missing 2026 climate target

Germany is on course to miss its legally binding climate target this year, according to preliminary calculations by the Agora Energiewende think tank.

Greenhouse gas emissions fell by only around 7 million metric tons of CO2 equivalent in the first half of 2026, a decline of about 2% compared with the same period last year.

Agora estimates that Germany will emit around 635 million tons of CO2 equivalent over the full year. That would exceed the country's 2026 limit of 625 million tons.

Germany emitted 648.9 million tons in 2025.

Agora said the decline so far this year was driven largely by weak economic activity and high fossil fuel prices rather than structural progress on cutting emissions.

The think tank said the energy price shock triggered by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz had pushed up oil and gas prices and contributed to lower fossil fuel use.

Germany is required to cut greenhouse gas emissions by 65% from 1990 levels by 2030, equivalent to annual emissions of no more than 439 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent.

Agora said meeting that goal would require emissions to fall by an average of around 40 million tonnes a year.

Skip next section Leipzig car-ramming suspect charged with murder

Leipzig car-ramming suspect charged with murder

German prosecutors have charged a man with two counts of murder and 85 counts of attempted murder, nearly four months after a deadly car-ramming attack in the eastern city of Leipzig.

The 33-year-old German suspect is accused of driving a car at high speed through a busy pedestrian area in central Leipzig in early May.

A 63-year-old woman and a 77-year-old man were killed, while eight other people were injured.

Prosecutors said on Friday that the suspect is considered criminally responsible. A preliminary forensic psychiatric assessment found no evidence that he was incapable of criminal responsibility or that his responsibility was diminished.

The man had initially been placed in a psychiatric facility on suspicion that he was suffering from psychosis. Prosecutors have now asked for that order to be lifted and for an arrest warrant to be issued instead. Leipzig Regional Court has yet to decide on the request.

He has also been charged with 91 counts of serious dangerous interference with road traffic and eight counts of dangerous bodily harm.

Skip next section Germany's president pays tribute to Norway's King Harald

Germany's president pays tribute to Norway's King Harald

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has paid tribute to Norway's King Harald V following the monarch's death at the age of 89.

In a letter of condolence to Harald's son and successor, King Haakon VIII, Steinmeier described the late monarch as a great friend of Germany and a force for reconciliation in Europe.

"The strength and devotion that he dedicated to his country every day were unparalleled," Steinmeier wrote.

Harald had devoted his entire life to serving his country and its people, the German president said.

"Germany is losing a great friend, and Europe is losing a great reconciler," he added.

Harald died on Friday morning after more than 35 years on the Norwegian throne. He became king on January 17, 1991, following the death of his father, King Olav V.

Steinmeier's description of Harald as a "great reconciler" reflects the king's role in deepening the close relationship between Norway and Germany after decades of postwar rapprochement following Nazi Germany's occupation of Norway from 1940 to 1945.

Read more here about the death of Norway's King Harald V.

Skip next section German unemployment remains above 3 million

German unemployment remains above 3 million

The number of unemployed people in Germany remained above three million in August despite signs of an improving economy, official figures showed on Friday.

Germany's Federal Employment Agency said 3.061 million people were unemployed, 54,000 more than in July and 36,000 more than a year earlier.

The unemployment rate rose to 6.5% from 6.4% in July.

Adjusted for seasonal effects, unemployment increased by 4,000.

"Even in August, there is little momentum in the labor market beyond the usual seasonal pattern," Federal Employment Agency head Andrea Nahles said, adding that the subdued trend of recent months was continuing.

Unemployment first climbed back above three million in July. Joblessness typically rises during the summer, while Germany's weak economy has also weighed on employment.

There have recently been signs that the economic outlook is improving. The Ifo business climate index rose for a fourth consecutive month in August to its highest level in a year, while German exporters have also become more optimistic.

Skip next section Germany sees earliest-ever start to grape harvest

Germany sees earliest-ever start to grape harvest

Germany's grape harvest has begun earlier than ever recorded following an exceptionally hot summer, according to the German Wine Institute.

"It was the earliest start to the harvest ever in all wine-growing regions," institute spokesman Ernst Büscher said. "Some winegrowers even cut short their holidays for it."

The harvest has already included not only grapes for Federweisser — partially fermented young wine — and sparkling wine, but also the first grapes destined for premium wines.

Harvesting is expected to begin "on a large scale" next week.

Büscher said the main harvest was starting one to two weeks earlier than in recent years, which was already earlier than it was decades ago.

"Compared with 30 or 40 years ago, it's certainly four weeks earlier," he said.

The harvest could be completed as early as September because many grape varieties are ripening at roughly the same time.

"This will be a very fast harvest," Büscher said.

Growers are also picking grapes early to prevent sugar levels from becoming too high. More sugar generally produces wines with a higher alcohol content, while demand is increasingly for lighter wines with less alcohol.

Prolonged heat can also reduce the fruit acidity characteristic of many German wines.

entries.title: What next? Kurds say yes, Druze still say no to united Syria
entries.summary: The Druze minority in Sweida, Syria, is now the only group that hasn't accepted central government authority. How does the end of an independent Kurdish area impact Druze plans for a different, divided kind of Syria?
entries.content:
Syria

What next? Kurds say yes, Druze still say no to united Syria

August 28, 2026

The Druze minority in Sweida, Syria, is now the only group that hasn't accepted central government authority. How does the end of an independent Kurdish area impact Druze plans for a different, divided kind of Syria?

This week, Syria's Kurdish minority agreed to dissolve what had been their almost 14-year-long experiment in independent rule.

During the Syrian civil war, which began in 2011, the Kurds consolidated their authority over a large part of northeastern Syria, and wanted to maintain that after the civil war ended. But as Kurdish leader Mazloum Abdi said this week, "circumstances have changed."

Kurdish fighting forces, which go by the name of the Syrian Democratic Forces, or SDF, will now be integrated into the general Syrian military, and the oil-rich area they ruled will come under the authority of the central government.

All this means that Sweida province, home to much of Syria's Druze minority, is now the only area not to have accepted the authority of the central government.

End of idea of 'decentralized Syria'

There is no doubt that the change in the situation with Syria's Kurdish community will affect what is happening in Sweida, experts say.

When Omer Ozkizilcik, a nonresident senior fellow at US think tank, the Atlantic Council's Syria Project, met with Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri in early 2025, the Druze leader said he was in daily phone contact with Abdi.

"He said that they were coordinating all their efforts and that they had a similar political vision for Syria — that is, decentralized with autonomous regions," said Ozkizilcik. "He basically repeated the Israeli approach, where they believe Syria should be divided, with an autonomous zone on the coast for the Alawite [minority], for the SDF in the northeast, and then in the south for the Druze. That shows that al-Hijiri's political vision was highly dependent on his alliance with the SDF."

That idea is no longer feasible. "Basically it puts an end to this vision of a fragmented, weak and decentralized Syria," the Ankara-based analyst argued.

That is also probably the reason why, earlier this week, al-Hijri again emphasized the Druze ties to Israel, Ozkizilcik suggested.

On Monday in Sweida, al-Hijiri declared the Druze an "inseparable part of the state of Israel."

"Even in terms of our beliefs, we share common ground," he said.

​​​​​​But it's clear that having Israel annex Sweida would be very difficult for a number of reasons, including geography and demographics. Sweida is also still dependent on the central Syrian government. Despite it being impossible for government forces to enter the area, Sweida still receives public services, salaries, pensions, power and water from Damascus.

What caused the rift?

The exclusion of government forces began after intercommunal violence in Sweida in July 2025. Fighting started between Druze and Bedouin locals. Government forces arrived, ostensibly to quell the violence, but they too were then accused of attacking Druze communities.

A report by the United Nations found over 1,700 people died as a result of the clashes.

The event resulted in deep Druze mistrust of the new Syrian government. Even locals who had been in favor of a united Syria began to question whether it might not be better to have a semi-autonomous Druze state.

"There has been a complete erosion of trust," Lubna al-Basit, a Sweida activist, told DW. "Before discussing solutions, the reality today is that the government must be held accountable for the massacres committed in Sweida."

Another Druze, now based in the US but who wished to remain anonymous for security reasons, believes the new Syrian government is more radical than it looks.

"They're trying to behave in way that appeases the West," he told DW. "But you know, we have this joke. They're indicating to go left when they're turning right. For the Druze, the priority would be security, dignity and a chance for prosperity. I don't think many people see that as attainable under the current Syrian government."

In September, a road map to repair relations was formulated with Jordanian and American negotiators. But Druze allied with al-Hijiri rejected the plan, and the central government hasn't done much to bring July 2025 perpetrators to justice. In June, the UN's special envoy to Syria said no progress had been made on the road map.

Since last year, Syria's central government "has dealt with the [Sweida] issue on the premise that a large-scale military confrontation would not resolve the crisis," researchers at the Syrian Center for Security and Defense Studies, or MISDAD, wrote in a paper this month.

Any such confrontation "would have deepened the rift with the local community and given external actors greater room to intervene or exploit the tension. Therefore, the Syrian government opted for a more cautious approach, based on calming the situation on one hand, and utilizing the state's security, administrative, and economic tools on the other."

Basically, the researchers at MISDAD continued, the Syrian government is waiting it out, hoping that increasing prosperity elsewhere in the country and the problems al-Hijiri's factions already have running the province's public services, will bring Sweida back to the fold.

A 'small authoritarian regime in Sweida'

What isn't likely to happen is any kind of revolution, Ozkizilcik explained.

"The issue here is that al-Hijiri has the guns, Israeli financial support and Israeli military advisers from the Israeli-Druze community," he continued. "There is basically a small authoritarian regime in Sweida that's controlled by al-Hijiri, so it would be very difficult for the Druze community to rise up against him."

Opponents of al-Hijiri have been forced out of the province, abducted or killed, there's been fighting between different Druze militias, and there have even been some small civilian protests. Reports say al-Hijiri loyalists have also stopped Druze civil servants from working with ministries in Damascus.

Ozkizilcik and other observers believe a resolution to the situation in Sweida won't come down to what al-Hijiri wants anyway.

Just as American military support — or rather, its withdrawal — for Kurdish forces was integral to the new resolution between the central government and Syrian Kurdish forces, what happens with the Druze community next is also likely to come down to external forces.

Some have argued that the situation in Sweida was a way for Israel to pressure Syria as the two governments tried to negotiate a new security agreement. Throughout 2025, senior Syrian and Israeli politicians were involved in talks, with mediation from the US, to potentially reactivate a 1974 disengagement agreement. However, these fell apart late last year.

Since the overthrow of the dictatorial Assad regime in Syria in late December 2024, the US has said it is in favor of a unified Syria. Israel appears to want the opposite, arguing that a divided Syria won't pose a threat.

"The real decision maker [on Sweida] will be Israel, not al-Hijiri," said Ozkizilcik. "Once — or if — there is a potential security deal between Syria and Israel, then I believe we will also see a political solution to Sweida and the Druze."

entries.title: Germany: Man gets life in jail for US tourist's rape, murder
entries.summary: The crime was unsolved for over three decades before new DNA proof made it possible to arrest and convict the now 81-year-old. His victim, Amy Lopez, was 24 at the time of her murder.
entries.content:
August 28, 2026

The crime was unsolved for over three decades before new DNA proof made it possible to arrest and convict the now 81-year-old. His victim, Amy Lopez, was 24 at the time of her murder.

A German court on Friday sentenced an 81-year-old man to life in prison for the rape and murder of a US tourist over 30 years ago.

Amy Lopez was 24 when she was raped and killed by the convicted man in 1994.

Hans S., whose last name is not given as per Germany's privacy laws, was only arrested earlier this year, when police were finally able to identify him using new DNA technology.

What do we know about the US tourist's murder?

Lopez's body was found near the historic Ehrenbreitstein Fortress in Germany's western city of Koblenz in September 1994 by children playing in the area. Her corpse bore stab wounds, severe head injuries and injuries consistent with strangling.

The regional court in Koblenz found that Hans S. had lured her into a secluded building, falsely promising to show her the way to a hostel, only to tie her up, rape her and then stab her nine times.

The court found that Hans S. had been "looking for a victim to rape" and that Lopez "was tragically in the wrong place at the wrong time."

The defendant confessed to the crime in general terms.

The courtroom was full of observers right through to the final day of what the judge called an "extraordinary case." Among those in attendance, were Amy's father and brother.

"Of course, the verdict cannot undo what happened, nor can it bring Amy back," said lawyer Kathrin Kienle, who represented the victim's family.

"But Amy's father and brother have told me that, in fact, they were never able to find any inner peace throughout this whole time whilst the perpetrator remained at large."

How was the defendant identified after 30 years?

The defendant had been known to authorities for other sexual offenses, serving prison sentences that lasted up to several years. Some of the incidents took place after 1994, with the most recent being in 2005.

His DNA had been on file since his 1999 conviction of attempting to rape a 16-year-old girl.

Though the genetic date had been later deleted, police managed to obtain a new saliva sample from the suspect, which matched a DNA trace found on Lopez's clothing.

His lawyer said he voluntarily provided the DNA sample because "he finally wanted clarity," describing his crime as "an enormous burden" on him.

The defendant was arrested at a nursing home in Koblenz at the end of February 2026.

After the verdict, defense lawyer Volker Klein said he did not intend to lodge an appeal or seek a review.

Edited by: Rob Turner

entries.title: Uganda: World's 'youngest monarch' dies aged 34
entries.summary: Oyo Nyimba, once recognized as the world's youngest reigning monarch, has died in his mid-30s. As one of Uganda's traditional monarchs, he took the throne of the Tooro kingdom in 1995, aged just 3.
entries.content:
Uganda

Uganda: World's 'youngest monarch' dies aged 34

August 28, 2026

Oyo Nyimba, once recognized as the world's youngest reigning monarch, has died in his mid-30s. As one of Uganda's traditional monarchs, he took the throne of the Tooro kingdom in 1995, aged just 3.

Oyo Nyimba, a Ugandan king of the traditional pre-colonial kingdom of Tooro, has died aged just 34, the prime minister of Tooro announced late on Thursday. 

"It is with profound sadness and a heavy heart that I announce the passing of His Majesty Omukama of Tooro, King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV," Tooro's regional leader Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki said on social media.

What is the role of traditional monarchs in Uganda?

Uganda is a republic, ruled by a parliament and a nominally-elected head of state, longstanding President Yoweri Museveni, who's been in power since 1986. 

But the country retains several traditional monarchies that still preside over their kingdoms as they were constituted in the pre-colonial period. Their power is largely symbolic but they wield considerable cultural and social influence.

Although they were banned after independence from British colonial rule in 1962 by a republican president who said he wanted to unify the nascent country, Museveni reinstated the traditional monarchs in 1993.

Oyo Nyimba was arguably the most recognizable among them, not least because of his unusual story, taking the throne at the age of just 3 in 1995.

What did officials say about Oyo Nyimba's death?

Regional leader Akiiki said that the king had died late on Thursday, without giving a cause of death. He said an official statement with further details, including the funeral and mourning arrangements, would follow later.

He called on the people of Tooro to "remain united, calm and prayerful during this difficult time."

Akiiki also issued one surprising claim about the unmarried young king, who since a very young age had been seen as perhaps Uganda's most eligible bachelor.

"The continuity of the Crown is assured," he said. "His Majesty leaves behind a Prince as heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of the Tooro kingdom."

Ugandan opposition leader Bobi Wine also issued condolences online. 

Oyo Nyimba's death triggered an outpouring of grief online and widespread national coverage in Uganda.

Who was King Oyo Nyimba of Tooro?

Born on April 16, 1992, Oyo was the second-born child of the late Omukama Patrick David Matthew Kaboyo Olimi III and Queen Best Kemigisa Kaboyo, with two sisters.

He ascended to the throne of Tooro, an area in western Uganda near the border to Congo, in 1995 after his father's death.

His unusual status as a modern "boy king" led to considerable interest early in his reign, including from world leaders like former Libyan strongman Moammar Gadhafi, who repeatedly visited Tooro.

Oyo's mother was among his key advisers in his younger years, as was President Yoweri Museveni, who attended his coming-of-age 18th birthday party in 2010 in Fort Portal.

In 2025, the Guinness Book of World Records said he was still the youngest reigning monarch alive, its most recent renewal of the record.

He spent time in the UK at Winchester University to conclude his education. This time away from Uganda prompted a failed challenge to his position in 2015, when his cousin Prince David Kijanangoma declared himself the rightful king of Tooro, accusing Oyo of neglecting the region.

Oyo was known as a lover of sports, and a fan of London football club Arsenal. He took interest in causes including HIV prevention, environmental conservation, tourism and climate change, for instance when he embarked on a hiking expedition in the Rwenzori Mountains in 2022 to try to showcase Uganda's tourism potential and the risks of climate change.

Prior to the news of his death, a Ugandan government minister was quoted in local media as saying Oyo had been seriously ill and was seeking medical treatment in the US.

entries.title: Africa's aging autocrats fight to stay in power
entries.summary: As some of Africa's longest-serving leaders grow older, they are using different tactics to extend their rule. But age, succession battles and public pressure pose new challenges.
entries.content:
Africa

Africa's aging autocrats fight to stay in power

August 28, 2026

As some of Africa's longest-serving leaders grow older, they are using different tactics to extend their rule. But age, succession battles and public pressure pose new challenges.

Power can be seductive, and many who possess it want to hold on for as long as possible. The leaders of China and Russia, for example, cleared the way for additional terms years ago, and in the United States, the president occasionally speaks of another run for office, even though the US Constitution does not allow it.

From the perspective of Paul Biya, however, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump are still relatively new to office.

Cameroon's president has been head of state since 1982. In 2025, Biya began his eighth term — which is officially due to end on November 6, 2032, just a few months before his 100th birthday.

The 93-year-old has given no official indication that he intends to step down, and the position of vice president remains vacant.

Paul Biya in Cameroon: A loyal leadership circle with one weak spot

During his 44 years in office, Biya has built a stable network of loyal allies that keeps the machinery of government running despite his lengthy absences.

The 93-year-old has now spent two and a half months in Geneva, Switzerland, continuing to issue decrees and make personnel decisions from abroad. In mid-June, his spokesperson denied rumors Biya was receiving treatment in a hospital and stated that the president was in good health.

"There is continuity, but that also means there is little momentum for reform within the government,” Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at consultancy Global Risk, told DW.

And while Biya's power apparatus has helped cushion the impact of the president's long absence, that does not necessarily mean the most influential figures on the ground are united. After all, a post-Biya era is now in sight, and several of his allies are rumored to have ambitions of succeeding him.

"When everyone is lining up to potentially succeed Biya, it also means that the elites may begin challenging one another," Ochieng said. Such rivalry, she warned, could lead to major disruptions, including the possibility of a military coup.

Analyst Levi Mboushou recently voiced similar concerns on DW's AfricaLink podcast.

"Everyone feels the fear and uncertainty, but no one dares to look directly at it because we all have to deal with this repressive regime. You see something, but you say nothing. That is the situation in Cameroon at the moment," he said.

Yoweri Museveni in Uganda: Signs of a dynasty?

Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni is only slightly younger, both in age and years in office.

The 81-year-old has been president since 1986 and, like Biya, recently embarked on another term. His succession also remains unresolved, although his son, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, has recently attracted considerable attention as head of the military.

According to Ochieng, the dynamics in Uganda are complex, not least because military elites and the ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM) have their own internal power structures.

"Muhoozi has become the most visible figure primarily because he has a strong personality and enjoys the discreet backing of his father. His rise is not the result of support from either the NRM or the military leadership," she said.

Kainerugaba is increasingly emerging as a political figure, including on issues beyond military affairs.

In early July, he ordered the closure of several media outlets. At the time, a source from an international foundation who requested anonymity told DW: "We are witnessing a transfer of power to the president's son."

A similar development has been unfolding for years in Equatorial Guinea, where Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, who has ruled since 1979, appears to be gradually transferring power to his son.

Known by the nickname "Teodorin," he has served as first vice president since 2016 and now also controls the military.

In June, Teodorin announced the resignation of the entire government on behalf of his father. Observers interpreted the move as a sign that he is gradually becoming the public face of state authority.

Whether Museveni will actually arrange his succession during his lifetime remains uncertain.

Ochieng believes that, in the event of a sudden power vacuum, Uganda could either hold constitutionally mandated elections or follow a scenario similar to that seen in Chad in 2021.

Then-President Idriss Deby was killed in clashes with rebels. The constitution was suspended, allowing his son, Mahamat Idriss Deby Itno, to take power.

Emmerson Mnangagwa in Zimbabwe: Party before people

Zimbabwe also amended its constitution this year, making it far less likely that President Emmerson Mnangagwa could be voted out of office.

In June, both chambers of parliament approved changes extending the terms of parliament and the president from five to seven years. Even more fundamentally, the president will no longer be elected directly by the people but by parliament, where the ruling ZANU-PF party enjoys comfortable majorities.

In July, the 83-year-old Mnangagwa signed the amended constitution into law. However, the opposition and some constitutional experts argue that a referendum should still be held. The government, by contrast, considers the constitutional amendment process complete.

"We are not surprised," Chiedza Mlingwa, deputy spokesperson for the Constitution Defenders Forum, said at the time on DW's AfricaLink podcast.

"The only thing one could be surprised by is the audacity, nothing else. We have observed this pattern since independence in 1980: ZANU-PF works to stay in power. The party does not believe in relinquishing power."

Ochieng noted that countries such as Togo and Cote d'Ivoire have also implemented constitutional changes aimed at preserving power in recent years.

Meanwhile, in Senegal, a constitutional amendment is being discussed amid tensions between former allies at the top of the state, President Bassirou Diomaye Faye and Speaker of Parliament Ousmane Sonko, both of whom are significantly younger than the continent's other long-ruling leaders.

"Even when legal safeguards exist, if they are not designed in a way that guarantees citizen participation, public debate, civil society engagement, or oversight by other institutions, then it becomes possible for unilateral decisions to be made at the highest levels of government," said Ochieng.

The weakening of institutions to allow individuals to remain in power, she added, is not an African problem but a global one.

Lucy Riley contributed to this article.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Germany's grape harvest starts earlier than ever
entries.summary: Growers expect good quality but below-average yields following an exceptionally hot summer. It continues a decades-long shift toward earlier picking.
entries.content:
August 28, 2026

Growers expect good quality but below-average yields following an exceptionally hot summer. It continues a decades-long shift toward earlier picking.

Germany's main grape harvest has begun earlier than ever recorded after the country's exceptionally hot summer accelerated ripening across its wine-growing regions, the German Wine Institute said on Friday.

The record-early harvest continues a trend seen in recent decades, with higher temperatures affecting when grapes ripen, as well as their sugar and acidity levels.

Where and when is the harvest starting?

"This was the earliest start to the harvest ever in all wine-growing regions," institute spokesman Ernst Büscher said. "Some winegrowers even cut short their holidays because of it."

Harvesting is already underway across Germany's wine regions, from Saxony in the east to Lake Constance in the south.

The harvest has already included not only grapes for Federweisser — partially fermented young wine — and sparkling wine, but also the first grapes destined for premium wines.

The main harvest is expected to begin "on a large scale" in the first week of September.

Compared with recent years, the main harvest has begun around one to two weeks earlier, according to Büscher.

"Compared with 30 or 40 years ago, it is certainly four weeks earlier," he said.

Why is the harvest so early?

The hot, dry summer caused grapes to ripen unusually quickly, while many varieties are reaching maturity at roughly the same time.

That means the harvest is also expected to proceed rapidly and could be completed by the end of September.

"This will be a very fast harvest because almost all varieties are ripening at the same time," Büscher said.

Climate change has brought some advantages for Germany's wine industry over the years. Warmer conditions have allowed growers to experiment with grape varieties better suited to warmer climates and have made wine cultivation possible in some new areas.

But increasingly long and frequent periods of heat and drought also pose challenges.

Growers are closely watching both sugar and acidity levels. Leaving grapes on the vines too long in hot conditions can push sugar levels higher, producing stronger wines with more alcohol.

High temperatures can also reduce the fruit acidity that gives many German white wines their characteristic freshness.

What will the 2026 vintage be like?

Growers are pleased with the quality of the grapes harvested so far.

"The grapes are still very healthy," Büscher said, adding that this pointed to aromatic white wines. Producers are also expecting deeply colored red wines.

However, the overall harvest is expected to be below average because dry conditions have left grapes smaller than usual.

Significant rainfall in the coming weeks could accelerate the harvest even further.

Edited by: Rob Turner

entries.title: What 'The Odyssey' can teach us about climate chaos
entries.summary: The Bronze Age collapse may have started with a water crisis. Today’s droughts raise the unsettling question of whether it could happen again.
entries.content:
August 28, 2026

The Bronze Age collapse may have started with a water crisis. Today’s droughts raise the unsettling question of whether it could happen again.

Christopher Nolan's latest blockbuster has drawn tens of millions of viewers into a world of stormy seas and cities on fire.

Minus the monsters, that world is based in reality. "The Odyssey" — a post-Trojan War survival story — is set during the Bronze Age collapse of civilization.

A new study links that collapse to a severe climate shift. And the authors warn of "implications for the future."

Scientists have long known about a mysterious and severe drought that struck more than 3,000 years ago, overlapping with the disintegration of kingdoms and states across the Mediterranean.

Research published last month sheds light on the potential cause of that drought: A slow drying trend and a quicker natural cycle of dry weather stacked on top of each other.

By the late Bronze Age, the West African monsoon system had been shrinking for thousands of years, turning a green Sahara into desert. Less rain over Africa meant less over the Mediterranean. That trend amplified when the region hit a dry spell caused by natural climate cycles from the Atlantic, which saw the region swing between decades-long wet and dry periods.

Katherine Power, the Stockholm University scientist who led the study, said the environment at the time could explain the mass migration and conflicts of the Odyssey's era.

For decades, scholars have speculated on the reason for the large-scale movement during this time — which is also referred to as the period of the so-called Sea Peoples.

Archeologists argue that climate shifts could help explain the migration and political collapse at the end of the Bronze Age. The new findings add puzzle pieces.

"We don't know necessarily why those people moved," Power said. "But if we can say, 'hey, the climate was getting worse and worse to survive,' that could be a potential reason."

'A perfect storm of calamities'

And that, she says, is relevant to today. Europe's major rivers are at record lows, and drought is creating conditions for devastating wildfires as well as fueling historic crop-loss. That includes France's lowest maize harvest in 50 years.

The same cycles of wetting and drying from the Atlantic are still at play, but they're now happening in the context of a world that's heating as a result of humans burning oil, gas and coal. 

"I think it is even more alarming and even more of a threat," Power said.

But does what happened then give insights into what might happen now?

Eric H. Cline, archeologist at George Washington University, who wrote a book on the roots of the Bronze Age crisis, said drought and disease were part of the "perfect storm of calamities" that led to societal downfall.

He sees parallels to today. In an email to DW, he said "we should be very concerned" about climate change as a stressor for the collapse of civilization. "That fear is not too dramatic at all."

He added that on his most optimistic days, he believes "we will come to our senses and sidestep that possibility at some point."

Was there a trigger moment for the collapse?

Power's research sought to explore what patterns might lie behind isolated Bronze Age drought events.

They started by examining plant spores, ice cores, cave stones, and other natural records that pointed to drought. Then, she and co-author Stockholm paleoclimate scientist Qiong Zhang turned to modeling to get a broader picture.

Their model looked at the whole planet, overlaid with a grid, each cell covering a roughly 125-kilometer (78-mile) area. A supercomputer then calculated the conditions in each of these cells, for every month, across thousands of years. That let the scientists look at the entire Mediterranean.

"We're not now stuck with just one core or one cave," Power said. "We can see farther afield and build a whole picture."

What they found was not a single event that dramatically and suddenly changed the climate. Instead, shorter cycles of wetting and drying lined up with a longer warming trend.

"When we are looking for connections between climate changes and civilization changes, we often are looking for that big, huge, abrupt, catastrophic event," Power said, adding that it is "slow, gradual changes that push a society over a threshold.”

She said it could have been a steady fall in water supply that led to a slow decline in crops, which prompted people to migrate, triggering conflict.

"It doesn't take very much to push a society over the threshold that they're comfortable with," Power said. "What if you add something more to the mix? Maybe then that pushes you a bit farther, and you can't quite recover from that."



Edited by: Tamsin Walker
